---
title: "When the picture is given: Olympic rings"
---

![The five Olympic rings you'll recreate: the right colors, each in its proper place.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rstropek/ts-web-playground/main/exercises/0010-Basics/olympic_rings.png){width=360}

This time the picture is given, not invented. You'll recreate the Olympic symbol, the five interlocking rings that everyone recognizes: three rings in a top row, two more below, each in its proper color and its proper place. When you're done, your version should look just like the original.

With the house and the cat, you invented the picture yourself. If a window
ended up a little further left than planned, nobody minded. This exercise is
different. You'll draw the Olympic symbol, the five interlocking rings. Now
the picture is *given*, and your job is to reproduce it: the right colors,
the right sizes, the right positions.

This is a very common situation in real projects. A customer brings a logo,
a designer delivers a layout, a game needs an existing character, and the
programmer's task is to match the original exactly. Working precisely from
a given design is a skill of its own, and this exercise trains it.

## AI tutor {#sec-tutor-olympic-rings}

Reproducing a given picture exactly means measuring, computing, and checking. If
your rings won't line up, describe the problem to the AI tutor of this part
instead of moving numbers around at random.

{{< tutor tutor-introduction >}}

## A ring is a circle without a fill {#sec-ring}

You already know everything you need to draw a ring. A ring is simply a
circle where only the outline is visible:

- `noFill()` switches the filling off, so the inside stays transparent.
- `stroke` sets the color of the outline.
- `strokeWeight` sets the thickness of the outline. Give it a generous
  value, and the thin circle line becomes a bold ring.

Remember that these three commands are settings: they stay active for every
shape that follows until you change them. For the Olympic rings, you set
`noFill` and `strokeWeight` once at the top, and then only change the
`stroke` color from ring to ring.

## Find the pattern before you measure {#sec-pattern}

You could put your sketch on graph paper and measure the position of every
single ring with a ruler. That works, but take a closer look at the symbol
first, because it's full of regularity:

- All five rings have the same diameter.
- The three upper rings sit on one line, at equal distances from each other.
- The two lower rings sit on a second, deeper line, and each one hangs
  exactly halfway between two upper rings.

Once you see that, you barely need the ruler. Choose a diameter and a
position for the first ring, and the coordinates of the other four follow
almost automatically: same y for the upper row, a fixed step in x from ring
to ring, and the lower row shifted right by half a step and down by a fixed
amount.

Looking for structure before reaching for the ruler is a designer's habit
and a programmer's habit at the same time. Regular patterns mean fewer
numbers to invent, and fewer numbers mean fewer mistakes.

## The right colors {#sec-ring-colors}

Part of matching a given design is matching its colors. The five Olympic
rings are blue, black, red, yellow, and green, and p5.js understands all
five as color names: `stroke("blue")`, `stroke("black")`, and so on. Check
your result against the original image: if your rings are there but the
colors are in the wrong order, the symbol is still wrong.

## Your exercise: Olympic rings {#sec-rings}

Open the **Olympic Rings** exercise in the web playground. Sketch the five
rings on graph paper, use the regularities you found to work out the
coordinates, and then draw ring by ring, running your program after each
one.

One thing you may notice: in the real symbol, the rings don't just lie on
top of each other, they are *woven* together, each ring passing over and
under its neighbors. Ignore that for now and simply draw five overlapping
rings; the exercise doesn't count the overlapping order. Weaving the rings
properly is a much trickier puzzle, and it gets its own exercise a little
later in the course.
